background.definition: Cryptorchidism is the failure of one or both testes to descend. Clinically, it means that the testicle is not palpable within the scrotum.

list.listitem: Two percent to 4% of all term infant males.
Thirty percent of premature infant males.
Ten percent of cases are bilateral.
In a perinatal registry in Nova Scotia, Canada, prevalence of cryptorchidism was 75 per 10,000 male births. The rate remained stable over the 26-year timeframe.
By 1 year of age, the prevalence is 1% to 2%; this is same as in the adult population.

In a recent population database study in Sweden (2001-2014), the cumulative childhood prevalence of cryptorchidism was 1.8% (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.5-2.0). Prevalence was higher in boys born prematurely, small for gestational age, or with low birth weight.
Cryptorchidism is the most common genitourinary abnormality in males.

Based on a Danish population-based study, the 27,505 boys (3.1%) with cryptorchidism were more likely to be diagnosed with intellectual disability (Hazard ratio [HR] 1.77; 95% CI 1.59-1.97), autism spectrum disorders (HR 1.24; 95% CI 1.13-1.35), attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (HR 1.17; 95% CI 1.08-1.26), anxiety (HR 1.09; 95% CI 1.01-1.17), and other behavioral/emotional disorders (HR 1.16; 95% CI 1.08-1.26) than the 856,578 boys without cryptorchidism.
Undescended testes
Ectopic testes
Retractile testes
Absent testes

In a case series of 80 boys undergoing operative exploration for 87 non-palpable testes between 2007 and 2014, 46% were atrophic or absent and the remainder appeared normal; most (70% and 81%, respectively) were located in the inguinal canal.
Prenatal exposure to the endocrine-disrupting chemicals polybrominated diphenyl ether and dichlorodiphenyldichloroethylene are implicated in cryptorchidism.

Genetic factors. Authors of a meta-analysis of five studies found that androgen-receptor repeat polymorphisms in CAG and GGN (longer length) were associated with cryptorchidism. In addition, authors of a meta-analysis found the A allele of SNP12 in estrogen receptor 1 appeared to increase the risk of cryptorchidism in Asians.

Children with Down syndrome have an increased incidence of cryptorchidism. In a case series of 40 children with Down syndrome, 27.5% had cryptorchidism; maternal (OR 5.26; 95 CI 1.06-25.41) and possibly paternal (OR 3.89; 95 CI 0.91-16.73) smoking was associated with increased risk.
The pathophysiology is not well understood.

Testicular descent occurs during two hormonally-controlled phases in fetal development - 8-15 weeks and 25-35 weeks gestation. Disruptions in either phase causes a failure of a testis to descend, although mechanisms remain unclear.
The inguinoscrotal phase of testicular descent is androgen dependent and occurs between 25 weeks and 30 weeks gestational age.
For testes that are not palpable at birth, approximately one third will be found in the inguinal-scrotal area, about half will be intra-abdominal, and 15% will be absent or vanishing.

Both hormonal and mechanical factors are thought to be involved. Boys with cryptorchidism have increased gonadotropin and decreased serum inhibin B levels (produced by Sertoli cells) compared to boys without cryptorchidism; inhibin B levels rise following orchiopexy which may reflect improvement in the germinative epithelium.

Reduced fertility is a complication of cryptorchidism. The stem cells involved in spermatogenesis (spermatogonia) are of three functional types: Type Ad, Ap and B spermatogonia. Type Ad maintain the supply of stem cells for spermatogenesis and it is possible that understanding patient phenotypes with respect to spermatogonia will assist in choosing directed therapy such as adjuvant gonadotropin-releasing hormone.
The distance between the anus and genitals is shorter than normal in children with cryptorchidism or hypospadias in cases of endocrine disruption.
Maternal tobacco(OR 1.18; 95% CI 1.12-1.24) and alcohol use may increase risk.
Low birth weight also increases risk with prevalence of cryptorchidism at 100% in infants weighing <900 g decreasing to approximately 3% in infants weighing 2,700 to 3,600 g.

Screen for cryptorchidism during routine neonatal and well-child physical exams. B The American Urological Association (AUA) recommends continued monitoring as acquired cryptorchid testes are at similar risk for developing adverse histologic changes as seen in primary cryptorchid testes.

The USPSTF recommends against routine screening in adolescents and adult men for testicular cancer due to moderate certainty of risk but no benefit; they did not review evidence for screening males with a history of cryptorchidism. B
Most children present at birth with nonpalpable testes on routine examination. Diagnosis is clinical; imaging is not generally recommended. C
If bilateral undescended testes, consider referral for further evaluation, particularly if there are other genital abnormalities. C

list.listitem: Most children with cryptorchidism present at birth with nonpalpable testes on routine examination.

Some syndromes are associated with cryptorchidism (Prader-Willi, Trisomy 18, and Trisomy 13 among others), but most cases are idiopathic. There may be a family history of abnormal genitalia or infertility.
The presence of other genital abnormalities, such as hypospadias, increases the probability of an intersex disorder.

Knowing that an older child had a descended testicle at birth can help distinguish between a retractile testis and an undescended testis. A retractile testis sits in the inguinal canal and may be massaged into the scrotum if the cremasteric reflex is overcome.
In general, no diagnostic or imaging tests are routinely recommended for infants with this disorder.

Ultrasound may be useful prior to surgery to determine the best surgical approach. However, in a review of administrative and medical record data at a single institution of children who were referred for undescended testicle, whose who underwent ultrasound experienced an approximate 3-month delay in definitive surgical management and only 54% of cases had correct prediction of physical exam findings.

If testes are undescended bilaterally, further testing or referral to pediatric urology may be warranted given the slight risk of congenital adrenal hyperplasia in the cases of genetic females or other intersex diagnoses such as hermaphroditism.
An infant with an undescended testis should be monitored by serial examinations until 6 months of age. If undescended testis persists, refer for surgical evaluation.

If a patient has nonpalpable testes bilaterally, refer to an appropriate specialist for further evaluation for congenital adrenal hyperplasia or an intersex disorder such as hermaphroditism, particularly if there are any other genital abnormalities. Children with unilateral cryptorchidism and phallic anomalies, such as hypospadias or micropenis, should also be referred for evaluation.

If a child presents with a retractile testis, they should be followed up with serial examinations to make sure that the testes descends fully into the scrotum. This usually occurs by puberty. Rarely, the retractile testes can become undescended.
Treat with orchiopexy; preferably by 12 months of age. B
Consider treating adolescents and adults with orchiectomy, depending on the status of the other testis. C

Hormonal treatment, such as using human chorionic gonadotropin, is controversial. Several small studies and a systematic review support that it may improve fertility.
In addition, authors of two systematic reviews and meta-analyses found benefit of hormone treatment on testicular descent, with success rates of about 20% for luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone and 24% for human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), acknowledging increased side effects and unknown long-term effects of treatment.

However, authors of a third meta-analysis of 7 RCTs found hCG treatment no more effective than placebo and no significant differences in the effectiveness of hCG versus gonadotropin-releasing hormone treatment.

Others, including the AUA, argue that it is not recommended because of its poor success rates in inducing descent, unknown long-term fertility outcomes, and potential side effects. Some providers still use hormonal treatment in specialized populations.

Orchiopexy is the procedure of freeing the testis and implanting it in the scrotum. It is recommended for children between the ages of 6 months and 18 months if a surgeon experienced in young children is available.

The risk of infertility rises if the longer surgery is delayed. By 1 year, germ cell density is already decreased. By the age of 3 years, as many as 65% of affected testes have no spermatogonia. By puberty, there is virtually no spermatogonia. Studies have shown that if orchidopexy is done between the ages of 2 years and 12 years in individuals with unilateral undescended testes, fertility is not affected. Even if the patient was older than 10 years at the time of orchidopexy, it may be possible to extract sperm from the testicle(s) in cases of azoospermia.

In prepubertal boys, with palpable, cryptorchid testes, the AUA recommends scrotal or inguinal orchidopexy. AUA For prepubertal boys with nonpalpable testes, AUA recommends examination under anesthesia to assess palpability of testes. If nonpalpable, surgical exploration and, if indicated, abdominal orchidopexy should be performed.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 8 studies with 1376 children found trans-scrotal orchidopexy comparable to inguinal orchidopexy for all outcomes except shorter operative time with the former.

Redo orchidopexy in one institution was needed in 1.8% (68 children) and accomplished using either an inguinal or scrotal approach; there was no difference in complication rates but operative time for scrotal orchidopexy was shorter (53.1 vs. 84.6 minutes).

Orchiectomy, or removal of the testes, is recommended by adolescence if treatment does not occur earlier or for a younger boy if there is a normal contralateral testis and either very short testicular vessels and vasdeferens, dysmorphic, or very hypoplastic testis. By the onset of puberty, there is little to no remaining spermatogenesis in the affected testis. There is, however, potential for malignancy and risk of testicular torsion.
The major goal of surgery is to preserve fertility, reduce the risk of testicular trauma, and reduce the risk of torsion.
Although the risk of testicular cancer remains high in those with undescended testes, those treated with orchidopexy before 13 years of age appear to have lower risk.
Refer to pediatric urology if there are bilateral nonpalpable testes at time of diagnosis.
Refer to pediatric urology if there is unilateral nonpalpable/undescended testis at 6 months of age.
Most cases spontaneously resolve in the first few months of life. After 6 months, spontaneous descent is very rare. B
Fertility rates may improve with earlier timing of the surgery. B
Higher risk for infertility is seen among boys with bilateral cryptorchidism and those without evidence of normal maturation of gonocytes into Ad spermatogonia.

In one case series of 128 patients followed with ultrasound for up to 3 years following orchidopexy, structural testicular abnormalities, possibly representing severe damage, was seen in 20% of initial postoperative exams and decreased to 7% on follow-up exams.

In a follow-up study of 333 boys with non-syndromic cryptorchidism who underwent orchidopexy within the first year of life, 20% to 25% were found to be at risk for infertility based on hormonal and histological data; 21% had low serum inhibin B, 25% had reduced germ cells and 23% had no type A dark spermatogonia present.

In a study of 51 boys with a history of congenital cryptorchidism and 65 controls, although pubertal onset of testicular growth was similar (11.7 and 11.8 years, respectively), testicular size was smaller among cases.
Testicular neoplasm rates are increased. Older reports suggest a 20 to 40 times increased incidence. Newer data suggest a more modest increase with an absolute risk of 0.3%. B

There appears to be an increased risk of testicular cancer among men who had intra-abdominal testes or who have abnormal external genitalia, abnormal karyotype, and/or hypospadias, based on one review.
Testicular cancer rates decrease if orchiopexy occurs before age 13 years. B

The AUA recommends teaching boys with previous cryptorchidism to perform monthly testicular self-examination after puberty to facilitate detection of testicular cancer. As noted earlier, the USPSTF does not recommend this practice.
